title: Don't judge a book by its cover
instructions: Read the article about a Human Library event at a school. Complete the sentences (1–8) with the correct ending (A–K). There are two extra endings that you do not need to use. There is an example (0) at the beginning.
instructionsHu: Olvasd el a cikket egy iskolai „élő könyvtár” rendezvényről, és fejezd be a mondatokat (1–8) a megfelelő befejezéssel (A–K). Két befejezés felesleges. A 0. a példa.

passage.title: Don't judge a book by its cover
passage.subtitle: At Greenfield Secondary School's Human Library, the 'books' were people

blocks.text: Imagine walking into a library where you can't borrow any books – only people. That is exactly what happened at Greenfield Secondary School last month, when the school organised its first Human Library. For one day, the gym was used as a library, and the 'books' were twelve volunteers who were ready to talk about their lives.

The idea of the Human Library comes from Denmark, where the first event was held in 2000. Its aim is simple: to help people question their prejudices by having an open conversation with someone they would probably never meet otherwise. Each 'book' has a title, such as 'Refugee', 'Wheelchair user', 'Police officer' or 'Vegan farmer'. Readers choose a title from a catalogue and then 'borrow' the person for thirty minutes.

Students could ask any question they wanted, as long as they were polite. 'At first I was nervous,' admits Zoe, 15, who borrowed a 'book' called 'Deaf'. 'I didn't know whether I should speak slowly or loudly. But Martin, the man I talked to, was really funny. He told me that people often shout at him, which doesn't help at all, because he reads lips.'

Many of the 'books' said they enjoyed the day as much as the students did. Amira, who came to Britain from Syria eight years ago, said that the students asked better questions than most adults. 'Adults often only want to know about the war,' she explained. 'The students asked me what music I like, what I miss about home, and whether British food is really that bad.'

Not everyone was enthusiastic at the start. Some parents worried that certain topics were not suitable for teenagers. So the organisers, two English teachers, decided that students under 14 could only borrow some of the books, and they asked every 'book' to think carefully about what they wanted to share.

In a questionnaire after the event, nine out of ten students said they had learnt something that surprised them. The school is already planning another Human Library for next year – and this time, some of the 'books' will be students themselves.

options.text: was organised by a group of parents.
had been surprised by something they learnt.
was turned into a library for the day.
asked more interesting questions than most adults.
was not sure how to speak to a deaf person.
is to make people think again about their prejudices.
chose a title from a list.
does not help, because he reads people's lips.
did not let younger students borrow every 'book'.
